title: Life of a Request & REST Design
caps: get slash users slash forty two
slash orders slash nine ninety nine

scenes.say: You click, and a database row shows on screen. By the end, you'll trace every hop between, and design an API that survives a retry.

scenes.head: A restaurant in disguise
scenes.say: Interviewers love this one. Picture a restaurant. The diner is the client. The host desk sends the order to a free kitchen: the load balancer. The kitchen cooks: your app server. For ingredients, it goes to the pantry: the database.

scenes.head: GET /users/42, hop by hop
scenes.say: Now the real steps for get slash users slash forty two. The browser asks DNS for the address behind the name, like a phone book. Then it opens a TCP connection and does a TLS handshake, so everything is encrypted. The load balancer picks one healthy server. The app runs your handler, and sends one SQL query. The database returns the row, and the app answers two hundred with JSON.

scenes.head: Time each hop with curl
scenes.say: Time each stage with curl. Put three timers in a format file, then run curl with it. Each number is cumulative, in seconds. DNS was done at twenty milliseconds. TLS was done at one fifty five. The first byte arrived at two forty. The gap between two numbers is what that stage cost.

panels.code:
# fmt.txt
dns   %{time_namelookup}\n
tls   %{time_appconnect}\n
first %{time_starttransfer}\n
curl -s -o /dev/null -w @fmt.txt https://example.com

scenes.say: Your turn. Using those numbers, how long did the server take between TLS finishing and the first byte arriving? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: TLS done at 0.155 s, first byte at 0.240 s. Server time?

scenes.head: Where 240 ms went
scenes.say: Eighty five: two forty minus one fifty five. DNS cost twenty. Connecting and encrypting cost a hundred thirty five, the biggest slice. The server needed eighty five. Blame the network or the code? Now you know.

scenes.head: Inside the app: 404 or 200
scenes.say: Inside the app, the router matches the path and calls your function. One query goes to the database. No row? Four oh four. Otherwise it turns the row into JSON and answers two hundred. Forty two exists. Seven doesn't.

scenes.head: Follow-ups on the journey
scenes.say: Follow ups. Why a load balancer? To spread traffic and survive a dead server. Why TLS? It encrypts, and proves who the server is. It's slow? Time each hop, then fix the biggest. The mistake: skipping DNS and TLS, and saying only that the server returns JSON.

Encrypts + proves who the server is

scenes.head: A filing cabinet
scenes.say: Picture a filing cabinet. One drawer holds all orders, slash orders. One folder inside is order forty two. The path names the drawer or the folder. The verb says what you do: read it, add one, or replace it. Nouns in the path, verbs in the method. That's REST.

notes.text: nouns in paths, verbs in methods

scenes.head: Methods and success codes
scenes.say: Use plural nouns: orders, not get orders. Get reads and never changes anything. Post creates a new order, and answers two oh one Created. Put replaces the whole order. Patch changes only a few fields. Delete removes it, with two oh four and no body.

scenes.head: Status codes as code
scenes.say: Now status codes, as code. No item in the body? Four hundred: the caller got it wrong. The item already exists? Four oh nine, Conflict. Otherwise two oh one, Created. Three calls print four hundred, four oh nine, two oh one.
Your turn. A client reads slash orders slash nine ninety nine, and no such order exists. Which status comes back? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `GET /orders/999`, and no such order exists. Status?

scenes.head: Codes on the request path
scenes.say: Four oh four. The path is fine, but the thing isn't there. Four hundreds mean the caller was wrong. Here are all four on one picture. Two oh one: the post worked. Four hundred: bad input. Four oh four: missing. Four oh nine: a duplicate or a version clash.

scenes.head: Follow-ups on REST design
scenes.say: Follow ups. Four oh one or four oh three? Not logged in, versus not allowed. Five hundreds? Our fault. Put or patch? Put replaces everything, patch only the fields sent. Versioning? A v one prefix, and never break old clients. Mistake: verbs in paths, two hundred for everything.
rows: Not logged in vs. not allowed
PUT replaces all; PATCH only fields sent

scenes.head: One purchase, two orders
scenes.say: A shopper taps pay. The client sends post slash orders. The server saves the order. But the answer is lost on a bad connection, and the client sees a timeout. So it retries. The server saves a second order. Two orders, one purchase, one angry customer.

scenes.head: The naive server
scenes.say: The same thing in code. Post appends an order and returns two oh one. The retry calls it again. Print the count: two orders, exactly like the picture.

panels.code:
orders = []
def post_order(item):
    orders.append(item)
    return 201
post_order("book")
post_order("book")
print(len(orders))

scenes.say: Now a different method. A client retries put slash orders slash forty two, with the same body, three times. How many orders exist afterwards? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `PUT /orders/42`, same body, sent 3 times. Orders stored?

scenes.head: Is a retry safe?
scenes.say: One. Put sets a state, so doing it three times leaves the same end state. That's idempotent. Get and delete are idempotent too. Post isn't, so a retry makes two orders. The fix is an idempotency key: the client sends a unique key, and the server replays the first result for repeats.

scenes.head: Replay the first result
scenes.say: Now the server remembers keys. The first call with key k one is new, so it saves the order and records two oh one. The retry has the same key, so the server replays that answer and saves nothing. One order. The client makes a fresh key for each purchase.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What happens on an API call? DNS, TCP, TLS, load balancer, app, database, back. Why a load balancer? Spread traffic, survive a dead server. Slow? Time each hop.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How do you design a REST API? Plural nouns, verbs as methods. Creating? Two oh one Created. Bad input? Four hundred. Missing, or a clash? Four oh four, four oh nine. Four oh one or four oh three? Not logged in, versus not allowed.
rows: Not logged in vs. not allowed

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is idempotent? Repeating leaves the same end state. Get, put, delete yes. Post no. A retried post? Send an idempotency key, and the server replays the first result.
rows: Repeating leaves the same end state
GET, PUT, DELETE yes; POST no

scenes.head: Practice this week
scenes.say: Three exercises. Run curl with the timing format on a real site, and name the biggest slice. Sketch five routes for a library API, with the status code for each. And write a post that takes an idempotency key, then replay it.
rows: Sketch 5 routes + status codes for a library API
Build POST with an `Idempotency-Key`; replay it

scenes.say: So say this. DNS, TCP, TLS, balancer, app, database. I time each hop. Nouns in paths, verbs as methods, honest status codes. Post isn't idempotent, so retries carry an idempotency key.
